title: Quantum's Endgame Is Not Cleaner Qubits, It's Who Can Mass-Produce with Phone-Chip Fabs
dek: Quantum computing's endgame is not who has cleaner qubits, but who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at 100,000 laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.
why: The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores; the first half's physics primer is more educational, veterans can fast-forward.
who: Investors focused on quantum computing route selection, semiconductor process engineers, and security practitioners wanting to calibrate the quantum decryption timeline.
skip: Listeners already familiar with superconducting and ion trap principles can skip from 57:56 to 1:28:00.

points.h: Ion traps and superconductors need miracles first; silicon doesn't
points.body: To build a 100,000-qubit ion trap, you'd first need to invent the optical miracle of 100,000 laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a warehouse-sized cryostat; a million spin qubits only require standard 300mm silicon wafers, run through the same lithography equipment that TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race is not single-qubit fidelity, but whether the scaling path already exists in the industrial system.

points.h: Quantum computing is no longer about principles, it's about engineering
points.body: In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. This episode, FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, scalability and economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes—superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, silicon spin—item by item. Laying out the evaluation system itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition; you can't just talk about principles.

points.h: Superconductors aren't a technical failure, they're an engineering impossibility
points.body: Estimates show that 1,000 logical qubits require 10 million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequency crowding occurs, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconductors only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the show separates "technically strong" from "engineering infeasible"; a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

points.h: Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
points.body: Ion trap coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by Paul trap oscillation frequencies, making them about 1,000 times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to break encryption, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take only about eight hours. Long coherence time doesn't mean more work per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate time is a throughput disaster.

points.h: The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
points.body: A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says 10,000 qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take years; even with 100,000 physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, breaking RSA would take about three months. This number strikes both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is also never far away. To achieve "breakable within months," qubit count, gate speed, and error correction must all be met simultaneously.

points.h: Quantum companies' fate is in government contracts
points.body: HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies live or die by government contracts, and being acquired is not failure but a way for the technology to enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

points.h: A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it's image recognition
points.body: Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper could tune six electrons by hand, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition—when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes; Krishna's team uses DETR combined with ResNet and Transformer to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can auto-align them.

points.h: Silicon may not be first, but it will be the last to win
points.body: FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (assuming isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard, like transistors replacing vacuum tubes, because it's cheap and manufacturable.
